name: Cris Kocian
title: Experimental Constraints on the Origin of ^{13}C-Depleted Martian Sediments in Gale Crater
authors: Cris Kocian^{1}, Christopher House^{1}, Jennifer Stern^{2}, Steven M. Bates^{2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD, USA
abstract: In Gale Crater, the Curiosity rover found organic molecules with a wide range of carbon isotopic compositions. Methane (CH_{4}) released during pyrolysis by the Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument exhibits δ^{13}C values in the range of –137 ± 8‰ to +22 ±10‰. Ten of the twenty-four samples in this dataset are strongly depleted in ^{13}C (δ^{13}C < –70‰). Two hypotheses to explain this ^{13}C depletion with abiotic processes are 1) contamination of the derivatizing agent N-tert-butyldimethylsilyl-N-methyltrifluoroacetamide (MTBSTFA) and 2) photochemical deposition of formaldehyde (HCHO). MTBSTFA, which is present in the background of the SAM instrument, has a δ^{13}C value of about –35‰ and would produce CH_{4} if pyrolyzed. Alternatively, ultraviolet radiation in the Martian atmosphere photolyzes carbon dioxide (CO_{2}) into carbon monoxide (CO) depleted in ^{13}C with a δ^{13}C of approximately –150‰. If this ^{13}C-depleted CO is further photochemically reduced to HCHO it could deposit onto the surface and be detected by Curiosity.\nTo test these hypotheses, we simulated SAM pyrolysis conditions in the laboratory and measured CH_{4} production and carbon isotope fractionation from candidate compounds. Tetrakis (trimethylsilyl) silane (TKS) was used as an analog for MTBSTFA. Pyrolysis of TKS at low (75℃) and high (455℃) temperature cuts produced CH_{4} with δ^{13}C values from –49‰ to –43‰, which are not depleted enough to account for lower SAM measurements. In contrast, pyrolysis of HCHO at the same temperature cuts produced primarily CO and minimal CH_{4}. Despite lower CH_{4} yields, HCHO derived from ^{13}C-depleted atmospheric CO could reproduce the SAM δ^{13}C values if the isotopic composition of photolyzed CO is retained. These results support photochemically produced HCHO as a more likely abiotic source of the ^{13}C-depleted CH_{4}detected by Curiosity than MTBSTFA contamination.

name: Liz Tofte
title: Quantifying Seasonal Sea Ice Melt and Sediment Plume Development at Arctic River Mouths
authors: Liz Tofte^{1}, Anastasia Piliouras^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The Arctic is warming at more than four times the global average. This warming has led to significant changes in Arctic river hydrology, including increased discharge, greater sediment supply, and earlier spring freshet onset. These upstream changes affect the coastal zone – dynamic land–ocean interfaces where seasonal riverine and oceanic processes regulate primary productivity – making them particularly vulnerable to climate change. Coastal sea ice melt and sediment plume development are two seasonal processes that directly respond to freshwater, heat, and sediment export from rivers, yet they remain under-observed. Quantifying how these processes behave and change over time can provide insight into how the coastal zone is responding to changing hydrology.\nThis study investigates six major Arctic river mouths: the Yukon, Colville, and Mackenzie in North America, and the Ob-Yenisei, Kolyma, and Lena in Eurasia. The objectives are to (1) characterize typical seasonal patterns of coastal sea ice melt and sediment plume development, (2) assess changes over two decades, and (3) compare variability between systems. Sea ice and plume behaviors were analyzed using MODIS-derived sea ice products and MODIS imagery, respectively.\nResults show that river mouths follow two primary ice melt regimes: initiating directly at the shoreline *{or} at offshore flaw leads, suggesting differences in dominant processes driving coastal ice melt initiation. As temperatures continue to increase into the summer, sediment plumes develop, with turbidity peaking in early summer following snowmelt and occasionally in late summer due to storm-driven resuspension. Eurasian rivers show significant trends in sea ice behavior, including a shortening melt season at the Lena and Ob–Yenisei and earlier landfast melt at the Kolyma. Across all systems, sediment delivery to the coast is occurring earlier, with significantly earlier plume onset at the Lena, Kolyma, and Mackenzie. Overall, Arctic coastal processes are shifting in response to rapid warming, though the magnitude and timing of change vary among river systems, reflecting strong local controls.

name: Renan Beckman
title: Exploring zircon dark zones through cathodoluminescence and trace elements: New insights from the Ruby Star Granodiorite, Arizona
authors: Renan Beckman^{1}, Herve Rezeau^{2}, Erik Schoonover^{1}, Maureen Feineman^{1}, Jesse Reimink^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Earth Resources Laboratory, Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
abstract: Copper is critical to the global energy transition, and demand is rising rapidly. The main global copper sources are Porphyry Copper Deposits (PCDs). New PCDs are becoming more challenging to find, and major discoveries from the past decade are being found deeper in the subsurface. To improve exploration strategies, a holistic understanding of the processes that drive PCD emplacement is required.\nRecent work has focused on accessory igneous minerals (e. g. zircon, apatite) within intrusions associated with PCDs as recorders of magmatic and hydrothermal evolution. Zircon textural features revealed by Cathodoluminescence (CL) record variations in the chemical evolution through its characteristic oscillatory growth zoning. This study specifically focuses on zircon “dark” growth zones that are commonly observed in porphyry intrusions, yet poorly studied (e. g., Bajo de la All umbrera; Buretet al., 2016). In Bajo de la Alumbrera, zircon dark zones display anomalously high concentrations of uraniumand rare earth elements (REE), and are interpreted as relics of a mafic recharge event (Bur et et al., 2016).\nTo test petrogenetic models for zircon dark zone growth, and their possible usefulness as a geochemical vector for PCDs, zircon grains from the Ruby Star Granodiorite associated with world-class sierrita PCD were depth profiled via Laser Ablation Split Stream Inductively Coupled Mass Spectrometer (LASS-ICP-MS). Zircons from the Ruby Star Granodiorite commonly exhibit dark growth zones characterized by enriched U, Th, and REEs. After rotating these grains 90º and polishing to expose the depth profile, we use SEM imaging and electron microprobe analyses to evaluate the morphology and chemistry of zircon grains. Here we present these findings and discuss their implications for the petrogenetic mechanisms that form zircon dark zones in intrusions associated with PCDs, and evaluate their potential to better understand emplacement and as a geochemical indicator to identify “fertile” intrusions.

name: Lillian Miller
title: Using InSAR, SAR Offset Tracking, and GNSS to Investigate the August 28, 2020 Bedrock Landslide Within the Irazú-Turrialba Volcanic Complex, Costa Rica
authors: Lillian Miller^{1}, Dr. Christelle Wauthier^{1}, Young Cheol Kim^{1}, Cyril Muller^{2}, Esteban Chaves^{2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Observatorio Vulcanológico y Sismológico de Costa Rica (OVSICORI-UNA), Universidad Nacional, Costa Rica
abstract: The presence of landslides in volcanic settings is a significant threat, as large landslides on volcanic edifices can lead to cascading hazards, including smaller landslides, debris avalanches, or magma chamber depressurization. On August 28, 2020, the Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (OVSICORI) observed a landslide in a valley adjacent to Irazú Volcano. The landslide occurred within the Irazú-Turrialba Volcanic Complex outside of San José, Costa Rica. Turrialba, the second volcano within the complex and just 10 km from Irazú, saw renewed activity beginning in 2010 and continuing through 2022 and has sparked concern of potential reactivation of Irazú and associated hazards. The cause of this landslide is currently unknown, but the renewed activity at Turrialba hints that the landslide may have been driven by underground magmatic activity within the volcanic complex. We propose to leverage optical and radar imagery in tandem with Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positional data to answer: (1) was the August 28, 2020 landslide initiated by renewed magmatic movement below the Irazú-Turrialba Volcanic Complex? And (2) was subsidence a precursor to the landslide? We hypothesize that the landslide was not caused by renewed magmatic movement and that subsidence was a precursor to the landslide. GNSS results show the landmass experienced 3.5m of accelerating subsidence over three years leading up to the landslide, with4 m of subsidence occurring during the landslide. However, Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) analysis of Sentinel-1 C-band SAR data reveals> 1 m of subsidence across the same period, likely due to high rates of deformation, fast temporal decorrelation, and vegetation within the volcanic complex. Continued work is being done to leverage offset tracking with Planet optical data and high-resolution COSMO-Sky Med X-band SAR data to capture the displacement and more accurately match the GNSS displacement of the landmass.

name: Ethan Heidtman
title: Modeling and mitigation of riverine saltwater intrusion hazards using reservoir operations: a case study in thetidal Susquehanna River
authors: Ethan Heidtman^{1} and Antonia Hadjimichael^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1}Penn State University Department of Geosciences\n^{2}Penn State University Earth and Environmental Systems Institute
abstract: Multi-purpose reservoirs are critical infrastructure for the management of water resources, and reservoir operations must often balance multiple competing water demands. Climate change is an important threat to the resiliency of water resources in these reservoirs, as it can limit the efficacy of historical operations strategies as well as water demands and availability. The Conowingo Reservoir, a large multi-purpose reservoir located in Pennsylvania and Maryland along the Susquehanna River, has been managed actively for decades, yet current operating policies fail to adequately account for internal system variability and emerging threats to regional water resource reliability. Havre de Grace, Maryland, a small community at the mouth of the Susquehanna River, sources drinking water from the river, and during periods of low riverine freshwater flow and certain weather conditions, saline waters from Chesapeake Bay can intrude upstream, degrading public water supply and corroding infrastructure.\nTo address this emerging problem, we first develop a statistical model for saltwater intrusion at the Havre de Grace drinking water intake using historical discharge, tide, and wind data from 2007– 2024. Salinity responses to wind and tidal forcing under low flow conditions are rare and nonlinear, such as in October 2016, when drinking water exceeded the EPA Secondary Standard for Total Dissolved Solids for a 2-week period. These events highlight the need for targeted reservoir releases prior to and during salinity events, and results indicate that the model can identify intrusion-prone conditions more than 10 days in advance. Future work will incorporate this forecast model into a simulation-optimization framework for the Conowingo, training adaptive, state-aware, and dynamic release policies that release water from the reservoir downstream to flush out intruding saltwater while continuing to satisfy pre-existing regional water demands.

name: Arthur Lo
title: Analysis of Ground Deformation Preceding the December 2020 – May 2021 Summit Eruption at Kīlauea Volcano, Hawai’i
authors: Arthur Wan Ki Lo^{1}, Christelle Wauthier^{1, 2}, Young Cheol Kim^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Institute for Computational and Data Sciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The 2020 summit eruption at Kīlauea Volcano, Hawai’i marked a new phase of eruptive activity at Kīlauea’s summit following the end of the 2018 Lower East Rift Zone eruption. Seismicity and ground deformation had been reported prior to the eruption, including an intrusion beneath the summit caldera on 2 December 2020. To investigate the geometry and volume of the 2 December intrusion, we processed interferograms using ascending and descending orbit Sentinel-1 SAR data with acquisition dates spanning 2 December2020. To investigate long-term summit deformation prior to the eruption, we also processed Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) time-series ofKīlauea using data from Sentinel-1 satellites (January to mid-December 2020).\nFor the interferograms, we measured line-of-sight (LOS) displacements ranging from about 14 to -2.8 cm and 7 to-4.2 cm respectively for the ascending and descending orbit interferogram. We inverted the LOS displacements and modelled the intrusion using analyticsolutions for point source, rectangular dislocation, penny-shaped crack andspheroid models in an elastic half space. The deformation coincides with the location of a linear feature within the summit caldera, which suggests that deformation observed in early December 2020 could be associated with movement along a caldera fault.\nUsing the time-series, we found a steady increase in LOS displacement within the caldera. We separated the time-series into 3 periods: P1 (January – early November), P2 (early November – early December), and P3 (early December – mid-December). We observed distinct deformation patterns, including localized deformation within Halema’uma’u Crater during P1, a marked increase in displacement rates within the caldera for P2 and deformation likely associated with the intrusion in P3. The pattern of the localized deformation during P1 coincides with the location of the eruptive vents which formed during the December 2020 eruption. This may represent a pathway along which magma was transported for the eruption.

name: Dan Cove
title: Laboratory methods to constrain the habitability of extreme environments
authors: Daniel Cove^{1}, Chris House^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Habitability, an environment’s ability to support life on some scale, is a concept that is pervasive in our discussions of planets in outer space. Whether the focus is on distant exoplanets, neighboring worlds in our solar system, or the planet Earth itself at various points in the past, physicochemical conditions which constitute habitability are constantly redefined and speculated upon. One characteristic shared by each of these example locations is that they are not readily accessible *{in situ}, whether due to a spatial or temporal barrier. For observed or theorized environments in such places, the development of laboratory simulations is necessary.\nThis study develops a series of laboratory assays that can be subjected to simulations of exotic environments to constrain habitability along a continuum from a single aqueous biological reaction to complete cell division. The assay representing the low end of the habitability spectrum is activity of the bio essential enzyme phosphatase, which cleaves phosphate ions from larger substrates to eventually create ATP for cellular energy storage. Such enzyme activity can be observed and quantified in lab experiments using ^{31}P NMR spectroscopy and represents the minimum biological reaction for the host environment to be considered habitable. The higher end of the habitability spectrum is represented by the replication of a (likely extremophilic) bacterial cell. The survival and replication of a bacterial culture subject to simulated conditions can be monitored using both fluorescent dye staining techniques coupled with microscopy and labelled isotope incorporation coupled with Raman spectroscopy. Creating a reasonable lab simulation of exotic planetary conditions and using these habitability proxies to work from one end of the continuum to the other will allow for better understanding of habitability as we know it and help to clarify key astrobiological target locations across the solar system and beyond for future space missions.

name: Mingxi Hu
title: The Paradox of Cyclonic Storms in a Cold Pennsylvanian Equatorial Region
authors: Mingxi Hu^{1}, Paul M. Myrow^{2}, and Michael P. Lamb^{3}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University\n^{2}Department of Geology, Colorado College\n^{3}Divisionof Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology
abstract: Earth has experienced extreme past climates, and the Pennsylvanian equatorial climate has been widely debated: while traditionally viewed as warm, recent studies controversially suggested widespread cold conditions and low-altitude glaciation. One tool that has not been widely evaluated is the state of the sea, which is powerful as the state of the sea and ocean–atmospheric linkages are highly latitude dependent.\nWe conducted a paleo hydraulic analysis on storm-generated, hummocky bedforms preserved in marine intervals of the Fountain and Minturn Formations in Pangea’s palaeoequator. Reconstructed wave periods and fetch distances indicate the presence of large gravity waves formed under gale-to-hurricane strength winds. These bedforms therefore required cyclonic storms driven by high Coriolis vorticity and high sea surface temperatures. These results are at odds with a cold equatorial hypothesis, and challenge published paleolatitude estimates (<5 degree north) for the Colorado region, suggesting that Pennsylvanian tropical conditions were fundamentally different than previously posited.

name: Ava Spangler
title: Collaborative Development of a Pluvial Flood Model and Adaptation Strategies to Advance Resilience in Baltimore
authors: Ava Spangler^{1, 2}, Antonia Hadjimichael^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Climate change is intensifying the hydrologic cycle, leading to more frequent and severe rainfall-driven (pluvial) flooding in urban areas. In the mid-Atlantic US cities, aging and under-designed stormwater infrastructure is increasingly strained by these events, resulting in recurring damage to property and disruptions to transportation networks. In this study, we combine community engagement with hydrologic modeling to develop and evaluate potential urban flood adaptation strategies. Over a three-year period, local technical experts and community representatives met regularly to discuss flooding concerns, identify priorities, and co-develop adaptation strategies. These discussions informed the development of an urban flooding model (EPA Storm Water Management Model) for the Baltimore Harbor watershed, the focus location of this study. The flooding model integrates complex surface and subsurface stormwater infrastructure data, local expert knowledge, and community insights. We simulate stakeholder-prioritized adaptations, such as green and gray infrastructure strategies. Model results demonstrate that enhanced infrastructure maintenance is the most effective adaptation for reducing flood depths, but has varied effects across the watershed, and can increase flooding in some locations. Spatially concentrated greening provides limited benefit to the watershed as a whole, but moderate benefit in community priority areas. Together, these adaptations have the potential to reduce flood depths by as much as 58% in some locations, greatly reducing property damage and mobility impacts, primary concerns of stakeholders. Future work will implement robust optimization tools to search for adaptations which meet stakeholder objectives and perform highly under varied future climate conditions. This work contributes to the expanding literature on collaborative modeling and demonstrates that community-engaged approaches can enhance model credibility and generate more actionable insights for communities seeking to strengthen climate resilience.

name: Bailey Hoplight
title: Elevated CO_{2} Effects on Water Isotope Fractionation in Trees
authors: Bailey Hoplight^{1}, Max Lloyd^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, the Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Plant tissues and their oxygen isotope (δ^{18}O) compositions are considered valuable records of paleoenvironmental change, capturing shifts in key climate parameters such as temperature, water source, and water availability. Plant tissue δ^{18}O represents the combined influence of these processes on the physiochemical response of the plant, and this understanding has been leveraged to reconstruct temperature and hydroclimate conditions across the recent geologic timescale. However, it is important to understand how additional factors could confound this framework. One such factor that remains poorly constrained is the response of plant tissue δ^{18}O under varying atmospheric CO_{2} concentrations.\nThis study aims to investigate the effects of elevated CO_{2} concentrations on the δ^{18}O isotopic composition of plant materials. *{Ginkgo biloba} trees were grown in chambers for six growing seasons with CO_{2} concentrations ranging from 425 to 1000 ppm. δ^{18}O compositions were measured from both bulk wood and cellulose of latewood across multiple annual growth rings. If resulting δ^{18}O values are found to be quantitatively related to CO_{2} concentrations, then previous and future paleoclimate reconstructions based on the isotopic composition of plant tissues will require careful (re-) calibration to atmospheric CO_{2}.\nThis presentation will highlight preliminary results, emerging isotopic trends, and offer initial interpretations as to how these patterns relate to physiological responses of plants under elevated CO_{2} conditions.

name: Mila Matney
title: Orbitrap-MS Characterization of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons on the Asteroid Bennu
authors: Mila Matney^{1}, Kate Freeman^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The return of material from the carbonaceous chondrite asteroid Bennu by the OSIRIS-REx mission provides a unique opportunity to explore pristine organic matter sourced from the origins of the Solar System. Many classes of organic compounds have been identified on Bennu, including bio-relevant molecules like amino acids, nucleobases, and sugars. Aromatic compounds found in carbonaceous chondrites are of particular interests they are prevalent both in soluble and insoluble organic fractions and have diverse potential origins, ranging from cold interstellar chemistries to high temperature reactions in circumstellar environments in addition to reactions occurring post-accretion on the asteroid parent body. Previous analyses have confirmed the presence of 2-6 ring polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) on Bennu, with a greater proportion of smaller forms than in studied meteorites. We will further investigate these trends using Orbitrap mass spectrometry (MS) which combines high mass resolution and low detection limits to allow for accurate measurements in sample-limited situations, like that of Bennu. The quantification of major PAH species and overall population of aromatics will be reported on, in the context of other meteorite samples and the history of the Solar System.

name: Alejo Giraldo
title: Three new Atherospermataceae species fromthe middle Eocene add 35 million years to the family’s Australian history
authors: L. Alejandro Giraldo^{1}, Peter Wilf^{1}, Raymond J. Carpenter^{2 }
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}School of Biological Sciences, Adelaide University, Adelaide, SA, Australia
abstract: The southern sassafras’s (Atherospermataceae) are a small plant family of ca. 16 species, ten of which are endemic to Australia. Despite being a dominant element of Australian rainforests today, the earliest continental record of the family dates to the Plio–Pleistocene of Tasmania, thereby limiting interpretations of Atherospermataceae biogeography. Here, we describe three new Atherospermataceae species based on organically preserved leaves from the middle Eocene (ca. 41–38 Ma) Anglesea flora of southeastern Australia, representing the terminal phase of Gondwana. The fossils were examined using light, epifluorescence, and confocal microscopy, and compared with extant material, including all extant Atherospermataceae genera, using the literature, herbarium specimens, cleared-leaf material, and cuticle preparations. Based on leaf architecture and cuticular morphology, two species are assigned to the living genera *{Doryphora} and *{Laurelia}, while a third, characterized by a densely papillate abaxial epidermis not seen in any living member of the family, is placed in a new fossil genus. These fossils extend the Australian macrofossil record of Atherospermataceae by ca. 35million years, provide the only pre-Neogene evidence of the family in Australia, and show that Atherospermataceae were already diverse and well-established in southeastern Australia by the middle Eocene, during the final stage of Gondwanan fragmentation. The occurrence of *{Laurelia} at Anglesea provides direct evidence that the genus, now extant in New Zealand and southern South America, once extended across a broader range than its modern relicts and prior fossils indicate, and suggests that Australia could have acted as the source or “stepping-stone” region for *{Laurelia} in New Zealand.

name: Mingxi​ Hu
title: Decoding the Late Paleozoic Ice Age Paradox: Basin-Scale Filtering of Global Climate Signals
authors: Mingxi Hu^{1}, Elizabeth Hajek^{1}, Brian Kelley^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The stratigraphic record is our primary archive for understanding Earth’s climate history and dynamics, yet sedimentary basins are active filters that "shred, " amplify, or distort original climate signals. This challenge is particularly acute in icehouse periods, such as the Late Paleozoic Ice Age (LPIA), regarding its tropical hydroclimate, temperature, and atmospheric circulations. It remains unclear whether these contradictions reflect fundamentally different mechanisms to the Pleistocene, or our inability to read LPIA records across boundary conditions.\nI propose to resolve this ambiguity by systematically comparing two equatorial Laurentia basins: the Bird Springs (BS) passive margin and the Midcontinent epeiric sea (MS). While both experienced similar tropical climate, they differed in oceanography, terrestrial flux, and accommodation. By integrating lithostratigraphy, geochemistry (B/Ga for paleosalinity; CIA for weathering), and fauna assemblages, I aim to quantify how basin boundary conditions tuned climate records. I hypothesize that the restricted MS basin amplifies high-frequency, regional "noises "decoupled from global trends, whereas the open-marine BS basin provides a better-fidelity archive for global climate forcing. Further comparison to other PIA records from various latitudes and locations will test whether LPIA climate patterns (e. g., ITCZ shifts) align with Pleistocene mechanisms. This research establishes sensitivity baselines for comparing local vs. global sedimentary records, providing a critical framework for 1) reconstructing past climate, 2) predicting future climate with geographical differences, and 3) informing resource management.

name: Sabrina Ashik
title: Leakiness Variability in Arctic River Deltas from SWOT Water Surface Elevation Observations
authors: Sabrina Ashik^{1}, Anastasia Piliouras^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Arctic river deltas play a critical role in regulating the delivery of freshwater, sediment, and nutrients to the coastal ocean, influencing sea ice dynamics and coastal ecosystems. Discharge and sediment concentrations are often measured upstream at the delta apex, and how these fluxes are partitioned and redistributed across distributary networks remains poorly understood. Flow partitioning within these networks depends on their hydraulic structure, including the degree of lateral exchange between channels and adjacent islands. One metric used to quantify this behavior is channel-island “leakiness, ” formulated by Hines and Piliouras (2024), which represents the likelihood of water leaving the channel as a function of channel geometry and water surface gradient. Leakiness has been calculated for the Mackenzie Delta using historical water level and discharge data from gauge stations; however, its variability across Arctic systems remains poorly constrained at basin scales due to sparse in situ observations. In this study, we quantify temporal and spatial variability in channel-network leakiness across major Arctic deltas using remotely sensed Water Surface Elevation (WSE) data from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission.\nWe extracted SWOT WSE time series at apex and outlet locations from August 2023 to January 2026, used WSE as a proxy for water level, and calculated monthly leakiness values. We then evaluated the relationship between leakiness and discharge using the framework proposed by Hines and Piliouras (2024). Preliminary results indicate a consistent positive relationship between discharge and leakiness at both apexes and outlets, with stronger sensitivity at the apex locations than at the outlets. However, we observed large inter-delta difference, suggesting that leakiness-discharge relationships derived from a single system cannot be generalized across Arctic deltas. These findings advance our understanding of flow partitioning in Arctic distributary networks and establish a foundation for quantifying large-scale hydraulic connectivity from satellite observations.

name: Ash Keenan
title: Morphodynamic Variability Between River Delta Experiments With Identical Input and Boundary Conditions
authors: Ash Keenan^{1}, Anastasia Piliouras^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, the Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Flume experiments are valuable tools for simulating and studying complex sediment transport and morpho dynamic processes that are difficult to observe in natural environments. However, these experiments are resource-intensive and thus rarely repeated, raising questions about the reproducibility of results. This research utilizes a series of five identical experiments (Su1–Su5) repeated under the same input and boundary conditions in order to investigate the inherent variability between physical delta experiments. We examine variations in delta characteristics such as area growth, wetted frequency, perimeter/area ratio, shoreline roughness, and fractal dimension using overhead photography and 3D photogrammetry. Preliminary results show that area growth rates remain positive and approximately linear across all trials, reflecting constant progradation under uniform water and sediment input, though final delta sizes diverge slightly. Wetted fraction values are comparable among experiments (means ~0.40–0.55), indicating occupation of a similar partially channelized regime. Perimeter/area ratio exhibits a consistent downward trend as deltas expand, with small fluctuations driven by planform differences. In contrast, shoreline roughness reveals meaningful divergence: Su3 experienced a major late-stage channel avulsion that produced fewer, larger distributaries and a sustained increase in shoreline complexity relative to the other experiments, which were characterized by gradual channel migration and numerous smaller outlets. Fractal dimension captures greater similarity of the shoreline overall but also reflects elevated complexity in Experiment 3 following avulsion. Ongoing work will incorporate earlier experimental hours and analyze photogrammetry-derived digital elevation models to assess differences in slope and channel relief. Together, these results demonstrate that while many bulk morpho dynamic metrics are statistically similar under identical forcing, stochastic events can generate measurable divergence, underscoring the importance of replication in experimental geomorphology.

name: Laura Kelsall
title: Microtextural controls on the dissolution of monazite and zircon during biotite-dehydration melting
authors: Laura Kelsall^{1}, Peter Kelemen^{2}, Andrew Smye^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Columbia University, Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory, Palisades, NY, USA
abstract: Differentiation of the continental crust into an upper layer enriched in heat-producing elements (U, Th, K) and a complementary lower crust depleted in these elements is key for continental stability (e. g., Mareschal & Jaupart, 2013; Sandiford et al., 2002). Recent analysis indicates that ultrahigh temperatures (>900°C) may be required to effectively redistribute U and Th from the lower to upper crust (Smye &Kelemen 2025). Such temperature requirements are at odds with equilibrium thermodynamic modelling (Yakymchuck & Brown, 2014), and so the exact mechanism that accounts for this observation is uncertain.\nHere we test the hypothesis that mineral armoring modulates the dissolution of monazite and zircon—key Th and U carrier phases, respectively—in silicate melt produced during biotite-dehydration melting. We present microtextural and trace element geochemical observations from a suite of aluminous metasedimentary rocks (Ivrea-Verbano Zone) that preserve a record of partial melting under peak temperatures spanning the biotite-dehydration melting interval (700-900°C). Automated SEM mapping of thin sections reveals a strong positive correlation between biotite and monazite modal abundances. In the amphibolite-facies samples 8-27% of monazite is either included or adjacent to biotite grains whereas in granulite-facies and ultrahigh temperature samples that decreases to 0-22% and 0% respectively. The amount of monazite included in garnet increases from 3-10% in amphibolite to75% in ultrahigh temperature samples. Zircon abundance is poorly correlated to biotite but still shows a similar trend of decreasing association with biotite (15-44% to 0%) and increasing association with garnet (3-29% to 38%) from amphibolite to ultrahigh temperature samples.\nThese findings suggest that the textural availability of accessory phases imposes an important control on the flux of U and Th into silicate melt produced during anatexis. Prior to the consumption of biotite, included carrier phases may be shielded from interacting with melt; peritectic growth of garnet serves to sequester carrier phases in the residuum. Work is ongoing to incorporate this microtextural framework into a forward model describing the evolution of melt U, Th concentrations during biotite-dehydration melting and to explore implications for crustal differentiation.

name: Drew Moreland
title: Understanding how flow variability and sea level rise impact delta morphodynamics
authors: Andrew Moreland^{1 }, Liz Hajek^{1}, Anastasia Piliouras^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park PA, USA
abstract:
Global temperatures are rising, accelerating sea-level rise that threatens the stability of deltaic environments. More than 300 million people live in or near vulnerable delta systems, many of which already experience land loss, subsidence, and amplified flood hazards. Global warming is also influencing river discharge patterns, which can trigger more abrupt avulsions and potentially deadly floods.
Most existing studies have examined sea-level rise and flow variability independently. However, these processes often operate simultaneously in deltas, meaning their combined effects on channel mobility, sediment distribution, and avulsion behavior remain poorly constrained. This project aims to address this gap by experimentally investigating how sea level rise and discharge variability affect delta dynamics both individually and together.
My experiments will be conducted in the Sediment and Natural Dynamics Basin for Observation and eXperiments (SANDBOX), a controlled physical basin that allows direct manipulation of sea-level rise and discharge variability. Over the course of my M. S. research, I will conduct approximately nine experiments looking at how sea level rise and discharge variability will affect channel mobility. Stratigraphic analyses will follow to quantify differences in sediment deposition and avulsion signatures across runs.
My hypothesis is that rising sea levels and increased flow variability will accelerate shoreline change and increase avulsion frequency in deltaic systems. From this we will learn more about stratigraphic stacking patterns and have a better understanding of accommodation and sediment supply. By linking sea-level forcing with flow variability, it fills a key gap in geomorphology for interpreting natural deltas. The broader significance lies in improving hazard assessment and management strategies for vulnerable coastal regions.

name: Doni Anderson
title: Exploring Deltaic Stratigraphy in Arctic Environments
authors: Doni Anderson^{1}, Anastasia Piliouras^{1}, Benjamin Cardenas^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: River deltas leave deposits that hold a useful record of past environmental conditions. Arctic deltas on Earth provide insights about how ice cover and permafrost affects depositional patterns, potentially holding clues to constrain identification of ancient deltas that may have formed under the influence of ice. Despite its current presence and abundance, deltaic stratigraphy in Arctic environments has not been heavily explored, limiting our understanding of ancient deltas. We aim to fill this gap.\nWe used numerical models of deltamorphodynamics in Arctic conditions to examine how permafrost and ice impact delta stratigraphy. We used stratal volumes produced by these models to explore differences between permafrost at varying erodibilities and different ice thicknesses (no permafrost to 65% permafrost erodibility and no ice to 4.5m ice thickness), and to quantify sand fraction throughout the delta. Preliminary results show that ice and permafrost have a noticeable impact on delta formation. As ice thickness increases and permafrost erodibility decreases, there is an increase in mud in the delta plain, likely resulting from sand being bypassed out of the subaerial system because the permafrost inhibits accommodation for the sediment supply. Sand fraction generally decreases down delta, but the combination of thicker ice and lower permafrost erodibility results in a shallower decrease in sand fraction in comparison with thinner ice/higher permafrost erodibility or no ice/no permafrost model run outputs. Whence thickness decreases and permafrost erodibility increases, there is more mixing of the mud and sand sediment throughout the delta, resulting in a higher sand fraction overall. Future analyses will describe channel patterns by quantifying channel lateral mobility and vertical stacking and measuring channel geometry. This work will continue to explore the implications of these findings for connections between ancient delta stratigraphy and paleoclimate. These first steps could prove useful for ancient delta studies on places such as Mars where its paleoclimate is still uncertain.

name: Edo Nurshal
title: Fault Slip and Fluid Flow: Seismic Source Analysis of Slip Patches and Their Role in Fault Permeability
authors: M. Edo Nurshal^{1}, Junpeng Wang^{2}, Pengliang Yu^{1, 2}, Tushar Mittal^{1}, Derek Elsworth^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Fluid injections can trigger fault reactivation, microearthquakes (MEQs), and permeability changes that are critical for geothermal energy production and subsurface waste disposal. Recent studies have shown that fault permeability can be quantitatively predicted from the cumulative seismic moment released by MEQs. To investigate the physical mechanisms behind this relationship, we conducted laboratory fault reactivation experiments on a Utah FORGE granitoid sample and analyzed acoustic emission (AE) signals generated during stepwise increases in injection pressure. Frequency analysis of thousands of calibrated AE signals reveals that fault reactivation occurs through the activation of numerous AE source patches with millimeter-scale radii, far smaller than the fault surface of the sample. The cumulative area of these reactivated patches exceeds the fault area by approximately one to two orders of magnitude (~10–50×) during each pressure step. These results demonstrate that permeability enhancement is not driven bay single large slip event but emerges from the sequential activation and interaction of multiple slip patches that progressively establish a connected flow pathway.

name: Guilherme Zakarewicz
title: DAS–Geophone MASW in Permafrost: Lateral Variability and Implications for Subsurface Characterization in a Changing Arctic
authors: Guilherme Zakarewicz^{1}, Gabriel Rocha dos Santos^{1}, Tieyuan Zhu^{1}, Ming Xiao^{2}, Eileen R. Martin^{3}, Ziyi Wang^{4}
institutions:
^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{2}Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
^{3}Department of Geophysics, Department of Applied Math and Statistics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
^{4}Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract: Permafrost is a subsurface condition where soil or rock remains below freezing temperatures for at least two consecutive years, covering large portions of the Northern hemisphere and Alaska. However, recent climate changes are accelerating its degradation, resulting in subsidence, riverbank erosion, and infrastructure damage. Detecting and tracking permafrost change remains challenging because many traditional observations are expensive and invasive. In this context, geophysical methods offer a practical complement by identifying differences in the physical properties. For instance, elastic seismic wave speeds respond strongly to variations in ice and liquid water content.\nIn this study we compare Vs profiles derived from (i) a distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) fiber and (ii) conventional geophone arrays at five different locations in Utqiaġvik, Alaska. Since the DAS and geophones were not exactly co-located (5-45 meters offset), the comparison provides enough lateral separation to test spatial variability. Although some sites presented similar Vs profiles, others showed larger discrepancies, exceeding the uncertainty bounds (typical ΔVs of ~100–400 m/s). We interpret those differences as reflecting lateral heterogeneity at dozen-of-meters scales rather than differences in the acquisition systems. To provide a quantitative example of a physical parameter that could illustrate the observed differences, we apply a rock-physics relation to estimate ice/water volumetric content and quantify how much variability in water saturation would be required to explain the observed Vs differences (typical ΔSw of ~0.15). We also compare the Vs-derived saturation profiles with temperature-based estimates from power-law relationships reported by an independent study to check plausibility.\nOur results show that permafrost should not be treated as laterally uniform when constructing velocity models and interpreting time-lapse changes, especially in coastal polygonal tundra where we expect variations in ice content, salinity and porosity. Furthermore, spatially dense measurements are essential for interpreting apparent changes in regions with complex cry structure and hydrology.

name: Ula Filipowicz
title: Modelling the Subduction Interface: The Role of Cohesion in Fault Stability
authors: Urszula Filipowicz^{1}, Donald Fisher^{1}, John Hooker^{2}, Tushar Mittal^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University\n^{2}Department of Atmospheric Science, Environmental Sciences, University of Incarnate Word
abstract: Earthquakes are among the most significant geohazards on Earth, with the largest events occurring along subduction zones. The mechanisms responsible for unstable slip along megathrust faults are believed to be primarily controlled by friction, normal stress, and fluid pressure. These concepts are reflected by earthquake models, which typically assume slip follows the rate-and-state friction laws, where friction evolves in response to velocity stepping, but cohesion is not included in the calculations. More recent experimental work, described by the CNS model, has shown that cohesion might be an important aspect to consider when determining the type of failure that will occur along the subduction interface, highlighting how behavior of faults can be defined from grain-scale mechanisms. Based on this microphysical research whilst also challenging the current paradigm, the hypothesis of this study is that cohesion variations can trigger fault instabilities independent of velocity weakening.\nIn order to test the role of cohesion, a numerical framework called the MEFISTO (*{Mineralization, Earthquake, and Fluid flow Integrated SimulaTOr}) model will be used. By simplifying the problem to a zero-dimensional block, the separated effects of cohesion and friction can be examined and quantified. This will improve MEFISTO’s ability to simulate earthquake nucleation and strengthening, allowing predictions for how different variables such as temperature and strain rates during interseismic periods affect cohesion, which can impact slip behaviour and result in earthquakes. Once cohesion is incorporated into the full MEFISTO framework, the resulting forecasts of earthquake size and distribution will be compared with the Global Centroid Moment Tensor (GCMT) catalogue to evaluate the predictions of the model, and hence, the significance of cohesion in fault stability. Such results would develop understanding of subduction zones and guide future applications of the model directly to field observations and laboratory analysis.

name: Zach Baran
title: Stratigraphy and Paleohydrology of Fluvial Deposits Near Juventae Chasma in Mars’s Southern Highlands
authors: Zachary J. Baran^{1}, Benjamin T. Cardenas^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Sedimentary basin stratigraphy records information about a region’s past depositional environments. Ancient fluvial deposits on Mars are often found within regional or large-scale topographic lows like craters or along the margin of the northern lowlands. However, a recent study showed that abundant fluvial strata also exist in the southern highlands, suggesting that stratigraphic basins also exist in locations incongruent with the modern topography. One of these southern highland strata locations is Juventae Plateau (62.5°W 4.50°S). Previous studies have identified hydrated sulfate minerals in strata across the plateau, as well as ancient river channel deposits, suggesting past water, but stratigraphic relationships have not been quantified and a depositional setting to explain both features has not been put forward.\nWe used high-resolution satellite images and digital elevation models to map ridges previously interpreted to be exhumed river-channel belts based on exposed point-bar structures and stacking patterns similar to exhumed channel belts on Earth and elsewhere on Mars. We measured the thicknesses of layered beds and ridges and found that ridges are consistently thicker than the layered deposits. The total elevation range occupied by the ridges and layered deposits suggests over 250 meters of basin fill. We measured orientations of strata and found both relatively flat-lying beds and inclined, truncated strata, which we interpret as fluvial floodplain and bar deposits respectively. Dip direction and exposed point-bar structures suggest a paleo flow direction of north-to-south, which is notably opposite to the modern regional topographic slope.\nWe measured ridge caprock thicknesses to reconstruct paleochannel depths and to look for downstream changes in paleochannel depth, testing hypotheses for deltaic (downstream thickening) and terminal fan (downstream thinning) channels, further constraining the depositional setting. Reconstructed channel depths were also used to better understand water availability and climate during basin filling by reconstructing water discharge using established relationships.

name: Olivia DiPrinzio
title: What Factors Drive Farmers’ Climate Risk Perceptions? A case study in Chitwan, Nepal
authors: Olivia DiPrinzio^{1, 2}, Nicolas Choquette-Levy^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Under climate change, global crop yields are projected to decline significantly, with staple crops showing reductions of up to 10% per degree of warming (°C). Particularly, this reality is most impactful on socio-economically vulnerable communities, such as farmers in South Asia, whose incomes are predicted to decline by 28% annually on average due to climate change’s impacts. Concurrently, climate and agricultural policies worsen existing adverse circumstances by omitting community climate risk perceptions. Such policy frameworks fail to integrate community-specific risks, tolerance, and exposure, thereby threatening livelihoods reliant on agriculture. To date, there is a limited understanding of the effectiveness of risk-informed policies under climate change uncertainty, whether in standalone analyses or compared with non-risk-informed policies.\nTo address this gap, multivariate statistical methods were employed to examine the drivers of farmers’ hazard risk perception in Chitwan, one of Nepal’s most climate-vulnerable regions, using a 2022survey. Guiding this process, causal modeling identified three key feedback mechanisms hypothesized to govern farmers’ reported exposure: insurance levels, remittance income, and perspectives on farming as a livelihood strategy. Initial statistical analysis demonstrates the importance of groundwater and irrigation accessibility, the varied influence of demographic variables, and remittances’ minimal influence on the frequency of self-reported exposure to climate-influenced hazards, the last of which contradicts the proposed hypothesis of remittances’ impact. Our results demonstrate inherent variability in hazard perceptions, such that while certain drivers are relevant across all hazards, a more tailored approach to driver consideration is required. Consequently, a signal exists for hazard-specific policies, such as hazard-specific vulnerability indices. As these are initial results, next steps include statistical analysis of farmers’ perceptions of future risks, time-series analysis to provide a more nuanced view of variability imperceptions, self-reports compared against climatological data (e. g. SPEI), and an exploration of hazard-specific exposure policies.

name: Jasmine Walker
title: The Role of Fine Sediment in Channel Mobility Stratigraphic Architecture
authors: Jasmine Walker^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Understanding how fluvial systems respond to change and record the history of landscape changes is essential for sustainably managing ecosystems, remediating environmental contaminants, efficiently exploring for natural resources, and successfully mitigating risks associated with river movements and floodplain inundation. Rivers play a key role in shaping the modern landscapes we inhabit and the buried deposits that form stratigraphy, from which we interpret the history of surface conditions on Earth. The integrated effect of silts and clays on fluvial landscape dynamics is recorded in the stratigraphic architecture of ancient river deposits and can enhance or occlude fluid flow in buried aquifers and reservoirs. Understanding how fine-sediment supply impacts channel mobility, stratigraphic architecture, and subsurface fluid flow is, therefore, key for reconstructing paleo-landscape conditions and predicting the distribution and connectivity of subsurface reservoirs, aquifers, and potential geothermal and carbon storage sites.\nA key challenge in understanding the relationship between the supply of fine sediment and resulting stratigraphic architecture is the interplay between processes occurring at both spatially and temporally variable scales. I aim to close this gap through inquiry into modern rivers and ancient river deposits that assess the role of fine sediment in channel mobility and long-term channel stratigraphic architecture, or “stacking”, in sedimentary basins. Using a combination of remote sensing of modern rivers, subsurface (seismic and well log) observations of ancient river deposits, and numerical modeling, I propose to answer the following science questions: (1) How does suspended-sediment supply impact channel mobility in global alluvial rivers? (2) What is the relationship between fine-sediment supply, channel mobility, and channel-belt depositional architecture influvio-deltaic settings?

name: Ran He
title: Iron carbonate as a robust archive for reducing paleoenvironmental conditions: oxygen and clumped isotopes evidencefrom burial diagenesis
authors: Ran He^{1}, Max K. Lloyd^{1}, Brian Currie^{2}, Miquela Ingalls^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Department of Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
abstract: Siderite (FeCO_{3}) is a redox-sensitive carbonate mineral that is pervasive in the rock record and can enable reconstructions of ancient reducing environments on Earth and Mars. However, post-depositional processes like burial diagenesis and surficial weathering can alter primary isotopic signatures through dissolution and reprecipitation (δ^{13}C, δ^{18}O and T(∆_{47}), limiting the reliability of these proxies. Unlike calcite and dolomite, the susceptibility of isotopic clumping in siderite to overprinting by these processes is poorly understood. We hypothesize that siderite is more resistant to these processes than calcite during fluid-mediated diagenesis due to its lower solubility. To test this hypothesis, we analyzed siderite and calcite samples from the Paleocene Fort Union Formation in the Wind River Basin, Wyoming. We collected coeval terrestrial siderite concretions and cement from two outcrops and six drill cores spanning a range of maximum burial depths (1.5-3.5km) due to tectonics, allowing us to distinguish between water-rock alteration during burial diagenesis and surficial weathering.\nAll calcite samples yield elevated T(∆_{47}) temperatures (44.5±1.2°C to 55.9±2.6 °C) paired with low and variable δ^{18}O values (-18.9 to -11.2‰), whereas siderite from outcrops and shallow cores records plausible Earth surface temperatures (9.1^{+5.7}/_{-5.4}°C to 27.6^{+5}/_{-4.8} °C). °C). Two micritic siderite ∆_{47}from deepest core (3.5 km burial) however, shows elevated T(∆_{47}) temperatures (43.7±0.9°C to 60.2^{+4.9}/_{-4.7} °C), indicating resetting through recrystallization. Of these two altered siderite samples, one exhibits textural and chemical evidence of recrystallization during burial under scanning electron microscopy, while the other shows no petrographic signs of alteration. Combining T(∆_{47}) and δ^{18}O, water-rock interaction model suggests the altered siderite has experienced rock-buffered diagenesis (water-to-rock ratio<0.5), whereas calcite has experienced fluid-buffered diagenesis (water-to-rock ratio>1). Together, these results demonstrate that siderite δ^{18}O and T(∆_{47}) are more robust to burial alteration than calcite, highlighting the potential of siderite as a reliable proxy for ancient reducing aqueous environments.

name: Yusuke Kubota
title: The role of the mantle decompaction layer in Hadean volcanism
authors: Yusuke Kubota^{1}, John Rudge^{2}, Bradford Foley^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University\n^{2}Department of Earth Sciences, University of Cambridge
abstract:
How the very early Earth lost its internal heat remains a subject of debate. Early Earth may have been characterized by extensive magmatism due to a hot mantle, which then acted as the primary heatless mechanism, or been more volcanically quiescent, where heat conduction through the lithosphere served as the primary heat loss mechanism. The primary mode of early Earth heat loss would then strongly influence tectonics and crust formation, the long-term thermal evolution of the interior, and surface environments where life could originate in the Hadean or Eoarchean.
Our recent crustal evolution model suggests that mantle melt production and mafic extrusive volcanism must have been limited prior to 3.6 Ga to remain consistent with Hf isotope data. We hypothesized that these geochemical constraints require a 'quiescent Earth ‘with a low melt production rate (<0.6 mm/yr). However, the actual magma supply is governed by complex geodynamic factors: specifically, the mechanics of melt generation, ascent, and accumulation at the mantle-crust boundary. Understanding these physical mechanisms is critical, particularly when evaluating high-flux regimes such as heat-pipe tectonics, which may be incompatible with the low rates inferred from the geochemical record.
A critical phenomenon affecting this supply is the formation of a decompaction layer beneath the mantle-crust interface. Since the crust acts as a rigid thermal boundary, temperatures drop rapidly near this interface. Consequently, ascending melt encounters a freezing horizon that acts as a permeability barrier, causing it to accumulate. Within this zone, the decompaction layer and accumulated magma generate significant melt overpressure relative to the solid matrix, driving magma into the plumbing system and initiating ascent. Therefore, characterizing the dynamics of the decompaction layer is crucial for understanding the physical controls on melt supply.
Recent numerical modeling of Io, an active heat-pipe body, demonstrates that crustal thermal structure is controlled by the physics of two-phase melt transport. This model suggests that magma transport is driven by mantle overpressure at the decompaction layer but limited by solidification within the plumbing system. Applying this physical framework to the Hadean, we tested which mantle dynamics and temperature ranges are compatible with the restricted melt fluxes required by the geochemical record. Preliminary results demonstrate the existence of a decompaction layer, where both effective pressure and extraction rates increase significantly with porosity. By systematically exploring the parameter space, we identify the specific mantle geodynamic conditions required to align plateau melting tectonics with the Hf isotope constraints.

name: Oliver Neilson
title: Quantifying the timing and volume of volcanic degassing in deep time: A case study from the Sinemurian – Pliensbachian Boundary Event
authors: Oliver Neilson^{1}, Isabel M. Fendley^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
abstract:
Understanding deep-time climatic perturbations relies on quantifying the initial drivers them. Earth system perturbations are highly sensitive to, among other parameters, the timing and duration of volcanic degassing. Currently, these parameters are coarsely constrained, with volatile estimates coming from melt inclusion data and radiometric dating^{1}.However, recent work has highlighted the power of combining sedimentary mercury (Hg), a volcanic tracer, and Hg cycle box models to estimate the tempo and volume of volcanic degassing in deep time^{2}.
Here, we present a quantitative high-resolution degassing history through the Sinemurian - Pliensbachian Boundary Event (SPBE). This protracted negative “U-shaped” carbon isotope excursion lasted for over 4 million years in the Early Jurassic (ca. 190 Ma). We utilize over 1600 samples collected from the recently drilled core at Prees, Cheshire Basin, U. K., as part of the International Continental Scientific Drilling Program JET project.
The SPBE is broadly coeval with increase drifting from the break-up of Pangea, the opening of the Hispanic Seaway, and a pulse of volcanic activity from the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province^{3–5}, all of which may have contributed to its shape and duration. We quantify the tempo and volume of volcanic degassing during the SPBE using a geochemical machine-learning framework to isolate volcanically sourced Hg, followed by identification of the best-fit degassing scenarios using a global Hg box model. To see how this would affect the carbon isotope record, we use the best-fit degassing scenario as an input to a carbon cycle model. We compare the modelled record to the observed record and discuss major differences.
This novel method allows for a clearer picture of past climatic feedbacks and Earth system dynamics; quantifying past climatic changes and their drivers are essential for better contextualizing modern and future climate change.

name: Sam Williams
title: Quantifying sediment storage and evacuation in response to compound earthquake and typhoonhazards in the Liwu River, Taiwan
authors: Samuel Williams^{1}, Eric Kirby^{1}, Roman DiBiase^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: In steep, tectonically active landscapes, earthquakes and precipitation can generate large, episodic sediment pulses that transiently alter channel morphology. The timescales over which these pulses are evacuated, and the sensitivity of transport to large discharge events, remain uncertain. Understanding how sediment pulses propagate through boulder-dominated rivers is necessary for predicting the long-term evolution of active mountain belts. Because these transient responses influence channel longitudinal profiles and the pace at which rivers adjust to tectonic forcing, constraints on sediment storage and evacuation are essential for linking short-term events to long-term landscape evolution. A natural experiment is posed by the Liwu River following the 2024Hualien earthquake in the Central Range of Taiwan. This Mw 7.2 event triggered widespread co-seismic landsliding, and an intense subsequent typhoon season had multiple storms capable of triggering additional landsliding and mobilizing stored sediment. I will quantify spatial and temporal patterns of sediment storage and evacuation in the Liwu River using a multi-temporal dataset to test the following hypotheses: (1) sediment aggradation will be clustered downstream of major landslide and tributary inputs rather than uniformly distributed along the reach, and (2) reaches with greater pre-event boulder cover will retain sediment longer during floods.\nThis study leverages a high-resolution Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) survey conducted in 2023 that provides centimeter-scale orthophotos and 3D point clouds for baseline channel morphology. These data will be integrated with a time series of 10–50 cm scale resolution orthophotos and a repeat UAV survey to quantify bed elevation change, sediment storage, and boulder exposure from 2023-2026 across a ~4 km reach of the Liwu River. Together, these observations will provide new constraints on sediment residence time and the role of boulder cover in controlling sediment transport following extreme disturbances.

name: Chandan Sahu
title: How does composition variation affect mantle solidus and thermal evolution of rocky planets?
authors: Chandan Sahu^{1}, Bradford Foley^{1}, Aaron Wolf^{2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}SETI Institute, Mountain View, CA, USA
abstract: Understanding exoplanet interiors remains a challenge due to the inherent difficulty of direct observation. While their atmospheres are observed using advanced telescopes, interior modeling provides information about their interior structure, composition, and evolution relevant for interpreting atmospheric observations. Current models often assume an Earth-like mineralogy, however rocky exoplanets can come in ranges of different compositions. Studies from the Hypatia catalog and other stellar composition catalogues show that stars can have a wide range of elemental abundances, leading to diverse mineral compositions in terrestrial planets, as they reflect the refractory materials present in the host star.\nOur research investigates how variations in interior composition affect the mantle mineralogy and solidus, the viscosity and consequently the planet’s thermal history. The solidus, marking the onset of melting, is crucial for heat and melt transport. On Earth, olivine and pyroxene are the primary minerals in the upper mantle. Variability in elemental abundances in stars suggests planets may have diverse olivine-pyroxene (Ol-Px) ratios. We use the MELTS model to determine how different mineralogies affect the mantle's solidus profile. Our results indicate higher solidus temperatures for higher Ol-Px ratio. We then integrate the calculated solidii with the mantle adiabat and heat sources/sinks to simulate interactions between mantle composition, temperature, viscosity, and lid growth over geological timescales. We also model the viscosity using flow laws and creep mechanisms, to observe the behaviour with changing Ol-Px ratio. This helps us understand melt production, outgassing, volcanism, and other dynamic processes during a rocky planet’s evolution, aiding in predicting the thermal and geological history of exoplanets. Understanding these is essential for identifying the presence of tectonic activity and volcanism, and can create and sustain habitable conditions.

name: Christian Lundy
title: The Stabilization of Waste water-Derived Phosphorus in a Florida Keys, USA Karstic Aquifer
authors: Christian Lundy^{1}, Eleanor Spielman-Sun^{2}, Lee Kump^{1}, Miquela Ingalls^{1}, and Rachel Housego^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}SLACNational Accelerator Laboratory, 2575 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park, CA, USA
abstract: Submarine groundwater discharge is an often overlooked source of nutrient loading in coastal ecosystems. Phosphorus (P) inputs into ocean surface waters can cause eutrophication, leading to algal blooms and deoxygenation. Shallow wastewater injection in Marathon, FL injects up to 700, 000 liters of high-P treated wastewater daily approximately 30 meters into the Key Largo Limestone (KLL) aquifer for disposal. P concentrations are greatly decreased within the plume due to dilution, adsorption of P to the calcite lattice, and precipitation of P minerals. This P sink is under threat as rising sea levels cause saline intrusion into previously fresh aquifer regions, leading to P desorption and possible P mineral dissolution. This study aims to characterize the P minerals precipitated from KLL shallow wastewater injection to assess P sink stability under future saline intrusion scenarios.\nCarbonatecores were collected at three locations along a cross-island transect through the Marathon wastewater plume in September 2025. Adjacent monitoring wells were instrumented with conductivity-temperature-depth sensors to determine core salinity zones and water samples were collected for plume geochemical characterization. Thin sections from the cores were selected from fresh and saline aquifer regions and sections of varying secondary porosity. They will be analyzed using µ-X-Ray Absorbance Near Edge Structures (µ-XANES) and µ-X-Ray Fluorescence (µ-XRF) at the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Light source (SSRL) and Scanning Electron Microscopy/Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (SEM/EDS) at the Penn State Materials Characterization Laboratory to determine P mineral speciation. We hypothesize that more stable P minerals will be present in aquifer regions with lower salinity and less secondary porosity, as decreased groundwater residence time from preferential karstic pathways leads to decreased P mineral precipitation. This project holds important implications for P loading under future saline intrusion scenarios and can provide important geochemical constraints for reactive transport modeling of shallow wastewater injection.

name: Anthony Delgadillo Salas de la Tierra
title: Reconstructing Late Pleistocene/Holocene Fire–Vegetation–Human Feedback in the Lake Malawi Basin Using Core MAL05-2A
authors: Anthony Delgadillo Salas de la Tierra^{1}, Sarah Ivory^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Lake Malawi is an important sedimentary archive for understanding the long-term changes between tropical African climate, ecosystems, and early human activity. During the Pleistocene, East Africa experienced megadroughts causing permanent ecological reorganization between ~85-70 ka, shifting from Afromontane forests to miombo woodlands. It is unclear if the transition is solely a climate shift or if early anthropogenic fire-vegetation feedback occurred. Addressing this gap has been challenging due to chronological uncertainties and coarse sampling resolutions during the Late Pleistocene-Holocene transition. This project tests the hypothesis that early human fire use during the 85-70 ka transition created self-sustained ecological feedback that later intensified during the Holocene agropastoralism.\nThis project aims to analyze 56 sediment samples from core MAL05-2A, spanning the last ~123, 000 years with some intervals studied at a higher resolution such as a millennial scale. By utilizing pollen analysis to track vegetation changes with microscopic charcoal analysis to measure fire activity, this study will develop an improved understanding of environmental conditions in southeast Africa. Results are expected to reveal two major phases of fire intensification, the ~85-70ka transition and the Holocene. This fire intensification is suspected to be characterized by a continuous directional shift toward grass dominated savanna assemblages. This research aims to determine whether fire-maintained landscapes in Southeast Africa are a modern occurrence or a legacy of Pleistocene anthropogenic influence, providing a base line for understanding modern landscape degradation and ecosystem resilience under climate change.

name: Zach Loveall
title: Dual-Clumped Isotope Disequilibrium in Terrestrial Carbonates
authors: Zachary Loveall^{1}, Ellen Olsen^{1}, Miquela Ingalls^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Terrestrial carbonates preserve valuable paleoclimate records in their isotopic compositions. However, kinetic effects associated with dissolved inorganic carbon cycling, including CO_{2}degassing, absorption, and water mixing can shift isotopic systems out of equilibrium. Because isotopic equilibration in the DIC–H_{2}O system occurs over hours to days, rapidly forming carbonates may preserve transient disequilibrium signals, complicating paleoclimate records. Carbonates from the Green River Formation of Wyoming and Utah record lacustrine, wetland, and shoreline environments during the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, a warm interval characterized by elevated pCO_{2} and high temperatures. These deposits provide an ideal natural laboratory for evaluating how rapid carbonate precipitation records isotopic disequilibrium across terrestrial environments and facies. Petrographic screening and mineralogical analyses were conducted on stratigraphically constrained samples to assess diagenetic overprinting. We interpreted preliminary δ^{13}C, δ^{18}O, and dual-clumped isotope (Δ_{47}–Δ_{48}) values within the context of depositional and diagenetic history to characterize departures from thermodynamic equilibrium. Preliminary petrographic characterization and initial dual-clumped results suggest variability among facies that may reflect formation mechanisms rather than temperature alone. These results will refine interpretations of carbonate-based paleotemperature reconstructions and establish a framework for identifying and quantifying isotopic disequilibrium in terrestrial systems during past greenhouse climates.

name: Lara Williams
title: Investigating deep critical zone structureusing landslide scars in the Taiwan Central Range
authors: Lara Williams^{1}, Roman A DiBiase^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The Critical Zone (CZ) is the near-subsurface layer that integrates rock, water, air, and biotic processes; it is where bedrock is weathered and regolith is produced. The thickness of this weathered zone is dependent on lithology, climate, and erosion rate. Models indicate that weathering depths will be deeper in areas of slower erosion, as slower erosion rates will increase soil residence times and allow for deeper propagation of weathering. However, it is difficult to isolate the influence of individual factors, and the lower boundary of the CZ is difficult to study as it is often beneath tens of meters of weathered material.\nTo address these challenges and isolate the role of erosion in determining weathering depth, I plan to examine landslides cars in the Central Range of Taiwan that provide a unique window into the subsurface. The steep, rapidly eroding Central Range has a consistent climate and lithology, with landslides cutting directly into small patches of low relief topography found along the spine of the range. These landslide scars often expose the full depth of the weathered zone and extend into unaltered bedrock below. I plan to measure the depth of weathering in these scars using aerial photography and high-quality drone imagery obtained in 2024 from Mt. Qilai from which I will build 3D models of the topography. By using the slope of the low relief surfaces as a proxy for erosion rate, this will provide a first-order sense of how weathering depth responds to erosion.

name: Tsunami Sharmba
title: A Network Analysis of Administrative Callsand User Interdependencies in the Colorado River Basin
authors: Tsunami Sharmba^{1}, Dr. Antonia Hadjimichael^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The Colorado River sustains over 40 million people, 5 million acres of cropland, and a $1.4 trillion economy across seven U. S. states and Mexico. The basin faces mounting stress from chronic overallocation, prolonged drought, and accelerating climate change. Initial water allocations were based on flow estimates that exceeded actual averages by at least 3 million acre-feet, a structural deficit that has deepened as warming temperatures reduce snowpack and accelerate evaporation. As supply and demand diverge, the basin is approaching a governance crisis that current frameworks are ill-equipped to address.\nUnder prior appropriation, senior water rightsholders place administrative calls that curtail junior users during scarcity. These calls are the operational backbone of the system, but the patterns they produce regarding who curtails whom, how often, for how long, and under what hydrological conditions, reveal how climate stress propagates unevenly across a rigid, seniority-bound network of interdependent users. When one user's call restricts another, that stress can trigger broader adaptive responses such as water transactions, crop changes, and decisions that carry their own risks and tradeoffs. Understanding where those pressures concentrate and how they cascades essential for anticipating maladaptation before it locks in.\nThis research maps the structure of water user interdependencies in the Colorado River Basin using administrative call records from the Colorado Division of Water Resources. By representing users as a network, this work identifies which users and reaches are most vulnerable to cascading curtailment and where the system is most delicate. These findings will inform future efforts to build resilience into governance frameworks amida deeply uncertain and changing climate.

name: Jackson Saftner
title: Low-Cost Monitoring of Inert Gas Stimulation with DAS
authors: Jackson Saftner^{1}, Xinxin He^{2}, Tieyuan Zhu^{1}, Shimin Liu^{2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: High-density micro seismic monitoring is aproven tool for stimulation verification and reservoir surveillance, but conventional campaigns typically require a dedicated monitoring well or a large surface geophone array. Here, we evaluate distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) as a cost-effective alternative by analyzing a continuous dataset acquired during an inert-gas (liquid CO₂) stimulation at an onshore well site near Olean, New York.\nThe dataset was recorded on a fiber array attached to the same wireline used to deploy the stimulation tool to the target interval. This single-well setup avoids an additional monitoring well and still provides dense, high-sensitivity measurements. In the continuous record, we capture the stimulation pulse with high signal-to-noise ratio and a rich post-stimulation interval characterized by sustained changes in seismic energy and numerous broadband impulsive signals consistent with cracking or deformation episodes.\nTo enable rapid diagnostics, we develop a lightweight detection workflow based on multi-band energy attributes and STA/LTA triggering. Applying the workflow, we identify 732 candidate impulsive events and track the post-stimulation event-rate evolution, finding an Omori-type decay similar to earthquake aftershocks.
