We then add a simple source-location step to estimate first-pass locations for a subset of detections (58 events), providing stimulation-verification metrics that indicate fracture propagation to approximately 50 m from the stimulation well.

name: Gabriel Dos Santos
title: Distributed Sensing of Frost Quakes and Ice-Wedge Cracking in Utqiaġvik, Alaska
authors: Gabriel Rocha dos Santos^{1}, Tieyuan Zhu^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Ice wedge polygons are distinctive periglacial landforms that result from repeated cycles of ground contraction and crack infilling in permafrost terrains. However, the fracture events that initiate their growth remain poorly documented through direct field observations. In this study, we analyze thousands of short-duration seismic events recorded over two winters using continuous Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) in Utqiaġvik, Alaska. These events display clear body wave arrivals followed by dominant surface wave energy and broadband high-frequency content, suggesting shallow sources near the fiber. We found a strong correspondence between peaks in seismic activity and peaks in modeled ground thermal stress, derived from athermo-viscoelastic model constrained by Distributed Temperature Sensing (DTS) from a co-located fiber. These signals are interpreted as cryoseisms resulting from the thermal cracking of ice wedges during periods of intense ground cooling, commonly referred to as frost quakes. To investigate the spatial variability of these events, we apply Matched Field Processing (MFP) using both surface and body wave arrivals. The resulting maps reveal evolving fracture patterns across the tundra surface. In addition, we performed source mechanism inversion on a subset of near-field events to investigate whether their waveforms can be used to infer rupture orientation or mode. Our results demonstrate the utility of DAS and DTS for detecting and characterizing thermally induced fracturing in permafrost. By combining seismic and thermal analyses, we provide new insights into the seasonal evolution of subsurface cracking and ice wedge development in a rapidly changing Arctic climate.

name: Dayang Zhou
title: Listening to Arctic Sea Ice: Seismic Tremors as a Proxy for Ice Strength
authors: Dayang Zhou^{1}, Gabriel Rocha dos Santos^{1}, Jackson Saftner^{1}, Tieyuan Zhu^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Sea ice is a critical component of the polar system, supporting Arctic ecosystems and coastal communities, reflecting a substantial fraction of incoming solar radiation, and attenuating ocean wave energy by acting as a mechanical buffer along coastlines. Under ongoing climate warming, Arctic sea-ice extent has declined rapidly. Reduced ice cover increases coastal exposure to wave forcing, accelerating erosion and heightening the vulnerability of infrastructure and communities. Monitoring nearshore sea-ice stability is therefore essential for assessing coastal hazards and environmental change in the Arctic.\nIn contrast to remote sensing methods, which typically provide spatial resolutions of tens of kilometers and temporal resolutions of days to weeks, seismic observations offer continuous, high-temporal-resolution monitoring that operates reliably through polar night and severe weather. Seismic data are particularly sensitive to mechanical ice processes that are difficult to observe directly. Interactions between drifting pack ice and landfast ice generate distinctive harmonic tremor signals that can be separated from other seismic sources. In this study, we investigate the physical processes responsible for these harmonic features and explore their relationship to landfast-ice extent through analysis of fundamental frequencies.\nTo enable systematic detection, we apply a machine learning approach based on YOLO (You Only Look Once) to identify harmonic signals in the time–frequency domain. The detected events exhibit clear seasonal variability, suggesting strong links to the evolving state of nearshore sea ice. These results demonstrate the potential of seismic monitoring combined with machine learning to provide new constraints on coastal sea-ice dynamics.

name: Young Kim
title: Assessing Post‑Collapse Flank Instabilityat Anak Krakatau Using Satellite Remote Sensing
authors: Young Cheol Kim^{1}, Christelle Wauthier^{1, 2}, Thomas R. Walter^{3}, Semeidi Husrin^{4}, Herlan Darmawan^{5}, Daniel Müller^{3}
institutions:
^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{2}Institute for Computational and Data Science, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{3}GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences, Helmholtz Centre Potsdam, Telegrafenberg Potsdam, Germany
^{4}The National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN), Indonesia, Jakarta, Indonesia
^{5}Laboratory of Geophysics, Department of Physics, Facultyof Mathematics and Natural Sciences, Universitas Gadjah Mada, Yogyakarta, Indonesia
abstract: Anak Krakatau Volcano, Indonesia, experienced a major flank collapse on December 22, 2018, generating a tsunami that caused significant casualties. Prior InSAR studies showed more than a decade of instability on the southwest flank. This study investigates whether instability continued after the 2018 event. We used ALOS-2 and Sentinel-1 data spanning2019 to 2024. Due to ongoing eruptive activity and surface changes, three separate time-series were generated to ensure enough reliable pixels for InSAR time-series analysis. The key focus area was the southwest part of Anak Krakatau, where faster movement was observed prior to the collapse and most of the newly erupted material had accumulated.\nPost-collapse displacements show a strong gradient that aligns with fractures observed in drone imagery. To better interpret motion, we decomposed the InSAR time series into vertical and east–west components, excluding the north–south direction due to low sensitivity. The vertical displacement shows an exponential decay pattern, interpreted as compaction and consolidation of fresh deposits. To avoid this signal dominating source modeling, we limited geodetic modeling to later intervals of the time series. These displacements were then used in rectangular dislocation inversions to characterize the subsurface processes controlling post-collapse deformation.

name: Sierra Melton
title: Enhanced Grounding Zone Stresses at an Ice Cliff Compared to at a Freely Spreading Ice Shelf
authors: Sierra Melton^{1}, Byron Parizek^{1, 2}, Richard Alley^{1}, Sridhar Anandakrishnan^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, and Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Mathematicsand Geoscience, Pennsylvania State University, DuBois, PA, USA
abstract: Ice stored in the Greenland and Antarctic Ice Sheets largely flows to the ocean through fast-flowing outlet glaciers and ice streams, forming floating ice shelves when it crosses the grounding zone. Ice shelves are susceptible to melting, rifting, and collapse, which has been observed to speed flow of non-floating ice and to expose grounded ice cliffs that can retreat rapidly by iceberg calving, raising sea level. Most ice sheet models do not simulate coupled ice-shelf loss and calving-cliff retreat because of difficulty in modeling the governing processes at suitable spatiotemporal resolutions and parameterizing the sub-grid scale physics involved in these transition regions. With the Ice-sheet and Sea-level System Model (ISSM), we compare the 3D grounding zone stresses for a freely spreading ice shelf with those at an ice cliff for an idealized outlet glacier. At an ice cliff, lack of support from any further glacial ice in the down-flow direction causes a stress imbalance, compensated for by enhanced englacial stresses. These enhanced stresses should speed rates of glacial thinning and retreat for an ice cliff compared to a freely spreading shelf because they are occurring within the grounding zone rather than within the distal zones of the attached ice shelf. Even a freely spreading ice shelf underestimates cliff stresses by shifting stresses from the grounding line to the front of the shelf. Our results will ultimately help represent ice-cliff retreat more accurately in ice sheet models to improve sea-level rise projections.

name: Noshin Sharmili
title: Exploring the Depositional & Erosional Morphology of Jezero Crater
authors: Noshin Sharmili^{1}, Liz Hajek^{1}, Kathryn Stack Morgan^{2}, Ben Cardenas^{1}, Libby Ives^{3}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, CA\n^{3}Michigan Geological Survey, Kalamazoo, MI
abstract: The Jezero crater western fan, an exploration site of the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover, contains a record of paleoenvironmental conditions, sedimentary processes, and potential biosignatures. It has generally been assumed that the modern shape and extent of the Jezero western fan is the result of the interplay between a deltaic deposit and billions of years of wind erosion on the Martian surface. Fine-grained facies such as silt and clay would have been preferentially removed by wind erosion while rocks made of sand and gravel would have been more likely tube preserved.\nHowever, this hypothesis is not consistent with the modern shape and extent of the Jezero western fan. Specifically, the scarp that defines the current extent of the western fan is abrupt and does not coincide with a downstream decrease in grain size. Instead, observations made during Perseverance’s traverse across the crater floor and the Jezero crater western fan suggest that the strongest control on the present shape of the fanis the spatial distribution of a sandstone- and boulder-bearing sequence (“the Upper Fan group”) that is unconformably overlain on underlying fluvial and deltaic sediments and absent on crater floor. Boulders are impervious to wind erosion and would essentially armor any underlying sedimentary rocks from erosion. This study employed numerical models to investigate the factors contributing to the preservation of Jezero Crater’s western fan morphology and to understand the erosion rates affecting its formation and evolution. The experiments tested the hypothesis that the fan's shape was originally inherited from the lower Otis Peak Formation and later preserved by the erosion-resistant igneous boulder deposits of the upper Otis Peak Formation.

name: Caleb Norville
title: Impacts of Fire and Solar Radiation on Afroalpine Vegetation in the Rwenzori Mountains
authors: Caleb Norville^{1}, Sarah Ivory^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}EESI, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Previous work has elucidated the responses of Rwenzori Mountains Afroalpine vegetation to Holocene temperature and precipitation changes, suggesting that Afroalpine ecologies may be more insulated from the impacts of increasing temperature than lower Afromontane forest communities. Precipitation changes over the Holocene seem to correlate more closely to observed changes in vegetation recorded by pollen preserved in Afroalpine lakes. However, a large portion of the variance in the pollen data remains unexplained by these climate factors, necessitating the examination of other environmental or ecological factors as potential drivers of vegetation. Fire has been proposed as a major catalyst for rapid vegetation change in the Afroalpine zone, especially following a large wildfire in 2012. However, recent work has suggested that large Afroalpine fires were rare to absent across most of the Holocene, making the 2012 event unprecedented over the past 13 ka. Ongoing work is focused on understanding the record of vegetation response to this localized recent fire event.\nAfroalpine elevations produce harsh conditions for plants, where frequent cloud cover and frost limits plant growth, and high UV-B influxes necessitate adaptations to this damaging solar radiation. Plants actively respond to changing UV-B influxes during the growing season by regulating their production of protective UV-B absorbing compounds (UACs) which have been shown to be well preserved within fossil pollen grains. These UACs in selected pollen taxa can be quantified using micro-FTIR spectroscopy, providing pollen-based proxy for paleo UV-B influx. Changes in fossil pollen UACs can track orbitally controlled changes in solar insolation; however, the impacts of UV-B blocking cloud cover have yet to be examined. Ongoing work is focused on determining whether changes in cloud cover associated with the termination of the African Humid Period can be observed in fossil Afroalpine pollen, potentially providing a novel proxy for paleo cloud cover.

name: Eric Hasegawa
title: The effect of ring substitutions on aromatic carboxyl oxygen isotope geochemistry and applications tomacromolecular systems
authors: Eric Hasegawa^{1}, Jason Boettger^{2}, Katherine Dawson^{3}, Katherine Freeman^{1}, Max Lloyd^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality, Raleigh, NC, USA\n^{3}Department of Environmental Sciences, Rutgers University, Newark, NJ, USA
abstract: The position-specific oxygen isotope geochemistry of macromolecules such as lignin, kerogen, or meteoritic insoluble organic matter (IOM) can give insight into the origins and reaction pathways of different functional groups. These functional groups are dominantly associated with aromatic moieties in the macromolecular structures. However, it is unclear if and how functional group electronic properties differ due to substitutions on aromatic rings and how they result in different isotope geochemistry. An example is the oxygen exchange chemistry that can occur on an aromatic carboxyl group such as the one found in benzoic acid. In this case, the carbon is sp^{2} hybridized, which links the oxygen to the larger aromatic framework. We aim to answer the question: how do additional ring substitutions change the oxygen isotopic exchange chemistry at the carboxyl site, and how does this affect our interpretation of carboxyl group chemistry in natural samples? Initial density functional theory modeling suggests little to no difference in fractionation factors, and we follow these studies with physical equilibration experiments using methods developed in our previous study of phenol-water oxygen exchange. We reacted benzoic acid and vanillic acid with waters of known oxygen isotopic compositions at elevated temperatures, and we injected these solutions into our electrospray ionization-Orbitrap mass spectrometer to determine oxygen equilibrium fractionation factors (the difference between an equilibrated carboxyl group’s isotopic composition and the water’s isotopic composition) for these two molecules. Carboxyl groups can exchange their oxygen in low pH conditions, and therefore their isotopic composition, once corrected with a fractionation factor, will likely represent the isotopic composition of the last acidic alteration fluid to which they were exposed. The impact of additional aromatic functional groups will be used as an analog to better understand the impact of aromatic linkages in macromolecular frameworks.

name: Erik Schoonover
title: Linking Arc Granitoids to Ore Deposits through Fluid–Melt–Rock Interactions
authors: Erik Schoonover^{1}, Cole J. Stern^{1}, Renan Beckman^{1}, Rory Changleng^{1}, Evan Ritchey^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract:
Rising demand for key metals has placed increased focus on discovering new deposits in Earth's crust. Resources, such as Fe, Cu, and the rare earth elements, are fundamental for infrastructure, energy systems, and national security. Generating deposits large enough to be economically viable requires efficient crustal processes that mobilize and concentrate these metals of interest. Investigating the mechanisms of ore-forming processes is important, particularly, for developing new exploration targets and reducing the economic costs associated with ore discovery and characterization. Crustal ore deposits provide a partial view of these processes because they are the final product of multistage, complex processes. Deposits are often overprinted by successive mineralization events, strongly modified by post-emplacement alteration, and their source rocks are rarely preserved or exposed. As a result, the physical and chemical mechanisms of ore formation are difficult to observe directly.
Bridging this gap in deposit formation requires shifting focus from the mineralized deposits to the magmatic environments that generate them. Two major deposit types that supply strategic and critical elements are iron oxide-apatite (IOA) and iron oxide-copper-gold (IOCG) deposits. These deposits are exemplar models for metal concentration and mobilization from arc magmas. Competing models for these deposits suggest either that enrichment occurs through separation of an Fe-rich immiscible melt or through Cl-rich fluid flux that sequester metals from a crystal-rich magma. Therefore, without source context, the interactions and relative roles of fluid, melt, and magmatic rocks during metal concentration remains unresolved.
My current hypothesis is that metal-enriched, channel-like features in arc granitoids represent the preserved record of metal mobilization during the magmatic-hydrothermal transition.
These features could provide a means to directly link late-stage arc magmatism with ore-forming processes. The Tuolumne Intrusive Suite (TIS), CA, USA is an ideal setting, enabling clear observation of the parameters governing fluid-melt-rock interaction during the metal mobilization.

name: Emma Hartke
title: Holoceneclimate changes, ecosystem conditions & early human activity in the Central Mediterranean: a multi-proxy investigation
authors: Emma Hartke^{1}, Kate Freeman^{1}, Miquela Ingalls^{1}, Melissa Berke^{2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, Notre Dame University, Notre Dame, IN, USA
abstract:
Holocene records of environmental change capture the interrelated evolution of climate, ecosystems, and early human activity, especially as societies in the Central Mediterranean transitioned toward increasingly settled agropastoral lifestyles during the Middle Holocene. Disentangling the relative influences of postglacial climate variability and anthropogenic landscape modification remains challenging, particularly in this climatically sensitive region. Continuous sedimentary records from both terrestrial and marine archives were analyzed using multiple biogeochemical and climate proxies to reconstruct these parameters and relationships in the Central Mediterranean.
This work integrates organic (lipid biomarker, compound-specific isotope) and carbonate clumped isotope analyses from terrestrial (coastal Croatian lake) and marine (Aegean Sea) sediment cores to assess changes in vegetation dynamics, fire activity, human lifestyles, temperature, and hydroclimate across the Central Mediterranean. Together, these records capture coupled ecological, climatic, and human-driven changes across the Holocene (11, 700 kyrs–present), a period for which regional paleoclimate data remain sparse.
Terrestrial biomarker results (*{n}-alkanes, PAHs, fecal stanols, GDGTs) spanning the Middle Holocene indicate intensifying human activity coincident with wetter regional conditions, the combination of which led to a temporary, localized enhancement of microbial activity. To contextualize these results within the regional climate space, we applied proxies for temperature (GDGTs, carbonate clumped isotopes) and hydrology (compound-specific hydrogen isotopes) to both our terrestrial and marine records. Results indicate a warming, drying trend throughout the Holocene, with the Middle Holocene a ‘transitional’ period tentatively punctuated by alternating wet/dry cycles. Ongoing hydrogen isotope analyses will better constrain the role of changing hydroclimate conditions on landscape evolution and human activity in the Central Mediterranean.
By pairing biogeochemical indicators of climate variability, ecosystem conditions, and early human activity, this study1) provides a pathway for tracing the spatiotemporal evolution of human lifestyle modes during a period of transitional climate dynamics, and 2) highlights the sensitivity of Central Mediterranean landscapes to even modest climatic perturbations and anthropogenic impacts, offering a long-term perspective essential for assessing future environmental change in this rapidly warming, drying region.

name: Juliana Drozd
title: Lipid Carbon Isotope Patterns as Metabolic and Environmental Proxies
authors: Juliana Drozd^{1}, Katherine Freeman^{1}, Elliott Mueller^{2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}Department of Geological Sciences, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract: The chemical structures and stable isotope compositions of lipids preserved in the rock record, known as biomarkers (molecular fossils), serve as proxies for properties that can be used to reconstruct past ecology and climates. Reconstructions based on biomarker proxies rely on knowledge of how organisms, specifically primary producers, change their lipid production in response to growth conditions. Metabolic regulation triggered by environmental change is difficult to assess with the biomarker record. However, differences in the carbon isotope compositions between different types of lipids potentially capture signs of metabolic regulation because the flux of metabolites through branch points in biosynthetic pathways can control the expression of isotope effects by enzymes. Fluxes are regulated in response to an organism’s needs and its environmental conditions but are also subject to constraints from the organism’s physiology, including the compartmentalization of eukaryotic cells. We used metabolic reaction network ditopologies modeling and comparison to existing datasets to assess these signatures for green algae, haptophyte algae, cryptomonad algae, and diatoms. In many algae, fatty acid biosynthesis is upregulated due to environmental stresses like temperature changes and nutrient starvation. This results in a decreased difference in the carbon isotope compositions of fatty acids and phytol, an important isoprenoid lipid. For green algae, sterol biosynthesis is co-regulated with fatty acid biosynthesis, which results in sterols becoming ^{13}C-enriched relative to phytol when the algae are under environmental stress. We can potentially use the differences in the δ^{13}C values of different types of lipids as a proxy for environmental stress-induced metabolic regulation in eukaryotic algae. These findings for modern algacultures might be able to be expanded to the biomarker record to spot paleoenvironmental conditions that would have stressed ancient algal populations.

name: Em White
title: Reworking of Hadean crust: Evidence from µ^{142}Nd anomalies in later Archean crust
authors: Emily L. White^{1}, Michelle Jordan^{2}, Steven B. Shirey^{2}, Timothy Mock^{2}, D. Graham Pearson^{3}, William J. Davis^{3}, Jesse R. Reimink^{1}
institutions:
^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{2}Earth and Planets Laboratory, Carnegie Institution for Science, Washington, DC, USA
^{3}Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada
^{4}Natural Resources of Canada, Geological Survey of Canada, Ottawa, ON, Canada
abstract: Earth’s dynamic lithosphere sets it apart from other observable silicate planetary bodies, as it features active and mobile-lid plate tectonics. However, the evolution/onset of these modern-styled plate tectonics, which have shaped Earth into the habitable world it is today, remains a fundamental and widely debated topic in the Earth sciences. The rate of net-continental growth throughout Earth history is required to evaluate the evolution of these geodynamical processes. One consequence of tectonics is however billions of years of Earth history the continental crust is often altered, overprinted, and/or reworked. This has led to a paucity of ancient crustal material preserved at the surface, limiting our record of Earth’s earliest continental crust and making it difficult to evaluate crustal growth through time. However, developments in high-precision whole-rock analysis of the short-lived ^{146}Sm-^{142}Nd isotopic system allow us to trace anomalous signatures of ancient precursors in the products of later magmatism, enhancing this record.\nThe Slave Craton (Canadian Shield) hosts excellent candidates for observing ancient crustal reworking, due to its near-constant record of episodic Archean crustal growth. It features 4020-2850Ma gneisses in the Central Slave Basement Complex (including the oldest known zircon-bearing rock in its Acasta Gneiss Complex) and in the Tree River region. Additionally, 2650-2580 Ma granitoids occur across the province, with previous Pb-isotope and long-lived Nd-isotope data indicating derivation from both ancient and juvenile sources. We present µ^{142}Nd (^{142}Nd/^{144}Nd normalized to the bulk terrestrial composition) values of fourteen Neoarchean and Meso- to Eo-Archean gneisses from across the Slave Craton. Our results document a more widespread presence of Hadean signatures in Eoarchean crust than previously reported (ca. -16 ppm µ^{142}Nd), and some anomalous Neoarchean granitoids suggesting possible derivation from ancient crustal reworking. These results will test for widespread reworking of Hadean continental crust, improving our understanding crustal growth through time.

name: Rory Changleng
title: Disentangling Polygenetic Zircon Populations from Archaean Gneisses Reveals a New Eoarchaean Terrane
authors: Rory Changleng^{1}, Erik J. Schoonover^{1}, Cristy Stoian^{1, 2}, JoshuaM. Garber^{1, 3}, D. Graham Pearson^{4}, Yan Luo^{4, 5}, Jesse R. Reimink^{1}
institutions:
^{1}Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, PA, USA
^{2}Department of Geology, Colorado School of Mines, CO, USA
^{3}School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of St Andrews, St Andrews, UK
^{4}Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada
^{5}Ken Williams Radiogenic Isotope Geoscience Laboratory, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
abstract:
A principal limitation of our understanding of the early Earth is the paucity of samples preserved from this time. Only around a dozen locations worldwide retain crust from the Eoarchaean(>3.6 Ga), and the true ages of many of these ancient vestiges of our planet remain hotly debated. One of the best recorders of crustal formation and alteration events is the mineral zircon. However, distinguishing between multiple igneous and metamorphic events experienced by a zircon population within an Archaean gneiss defines a critical question: how old is this rock?
Each tract of ancient crust discovered carries a disproportionate significance in shedding light on the magmatic and geodynamic conditions shaping our planet's earliest evolution. Consequently, careful evaluation is required when assessing whether a terrane preserves such ancient lithologies. We present a new U-Pb zircon geochronology from three basement gneisses from the Eokuk Uplift, northwest Slave Craton. This region represents an excellent target to search for new remnants of old crust due to superb outcrop exposure, proximity to the 4.03 Ga Acasta Gneiss Complex, and its relatively understudied nature resulting from its remote Arctic setting.
All three gneisses are complex and polydeformed, with zircon age populations spanning more than 500 million years. We employ depth-profile analysis to target zircon rim domains and integrate these data with cathodoluminescence SEM imaging to aid in interpreting conventional LA–ICP–MS spot analyses. This combined approach allows us to reconstruct zircon crystallization and alteration histories for each sample.
Although Eoarchaean-aged zircons occur in all three gneisses, only one sample preserves a primary igneous zircon population recording the original crystallisation age of the host rock. At 3.81 Ga, this sample demonstrates that Eoarchaean crust is more widespread within the Slave Craton than previously recognized, significantly expanding the material available for studying the earliest chapters of Earth’s history.

name: Fran Meyer
title: Oxidized uranium in organic-rich shales from reducing environments
authors: Fran Meyer^{1}, Anthony Chappaz^{2}, Dan Gregory^{3}, Eve Carrothers^{3}, Erik Sperling^{4}, Justin Strauss^{5}, Lucien Nana Yobo^{6}, Kimberly Lau^{1}
institutions:
^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{2}Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, MI, USA
^{3}Department of Earth Sciences, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, CA
^{4}Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
^{5}Department of Earth Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
^{6}Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
abstract: The availability of oxygen in the Earth’s ancient ocean and atmosphere is a key parameter for understanding Precambrian and Paleozoic biotic evolution and nutrient cycling. Due to the lack of direct oxygen measurements in deep time, we must turn to the geochemical signatures preserved in the sedimentary record. The enrichments and isotope ratios of redox-sensitive elements deposited in marine basins, like U, provide a way to reconstruct changes in ocean oxygen availability. However, these proxies rely on many unverified assumptions of how their solubility, speciation, and burial are controlled by redox conditions. Currently, interpreting U in reducing marines hales as a paleo-redox proxy assumes that burial and isotope fractionation are only associated with the reduction of U (VI) to U (IV), and sequestration of U (VI) and U (V) is negligible. Yet, the burial pathways and speciation of U in reducing marine environments still need to be defined. Without characterizing the oxidation states or phase associations of U in marine shales, interpretations of the U-based proxies remain uncertain.\nIn this study, we use synchrotron-based X-ray fluorescence imaging and spatially resolved X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy (XANES) at the U L3-edge paired with high energy resolution fluorescence detection XANES at the U M4-edge to determine the spatial distribution and speciation of U in marine shales from multiple localities and time intervals. Samples included outcrop and drill core shales from the Cretaceous Eagle Ford Group, the Devonian Marcellus Formation, and the Ordovician Road River Group. XANES spectra at both the U L3- and M4-edgesuggest that three U oxidation states (IV, V and VI) are present, despite proxy data suggesting anoxic depositional settings. The ubiquitous presence of U (V) and U (VI) in marine shales from reducing environments adds new understanding of the U marine cycle and challenges the current use of U as a paleo-redox proxy.

name: Hanna Leapaldt
title: Signatures of microbial carbon cyclingin magnesium carbonate minerals
authors: Hanna C. Leapaldt^{1}, Tori C. Cassady^{2}, Frank A. Corsetti^{2}, Miquela Ingalls^{1}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, Pennsylvania, 16802, USA\n^{2}Department of Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, California, 90089, USA
abstract: Magnesium carbonate minerals have been identified in the Jezero Crater paleolake basin on Mars and have been collected by *{Perseverance} to be evaluated for potential biosignatures. However, there is not yet a diagnostic set of textural, geochemical, and isotopic characteristics that can distinguish biotic from abiotic magnesium carbonate minerals. We compared magnesium carbonate samples that form biotically – from microbial mats and shallow sediments in two hyperalkaline lake/playa systems in British Columbia (South Atlin Playa and Alberta Lake) – to those forming abiotically from carbonation of serpentinite in bedrock. We used a novel isotope system (dual-clumped isotopes; Δ_{47}-Δ_{48}) and hypothesized that biological carbon cycling within the microbial mats will cause kinetic isotope effects resulting in Δ_{47}-Δ_{48}disequilibrium signatures. We measured the Δ_{47}and Δ_{48}values every 5 cm of 15 cm cores through the microbial mats as well as from the subsampled bedrock. All microbial mat cores revealed the same, distinctive trend with depth: the Δ_{47}-Δ_{48} values of samples in the upper 5 cm of the cores within microbial mat, where we expect active cyanobacterial photosynthesis, yielded the largest offset from the Δ_{47}-Δ_{48}theoretical equilibrium. The microbial mat sample Δ_{47}-Δ_{48}values yield disequilibrium signatures expected for association with photoautotrophy. We interpret the observed values to be a signature of cyanobacterial photosynthesis at the mat surface causing CO2 degassing, leading to the observed -Δ_{47}/+Δ_{48} kinetic isotope effects. Fluorescently labelled embedded core images from the upper 5cm at both locations reveal cellular material incorporated into the fabric of the sediment, providing evidence of a microbial control on carbon cycling. If such kinetic isotope effects are absent from abiotically formed magnesium carbonate minerals, dual-clumped isotopes can provide a tool to help identify biogenicity of magnesium carbonate minerals when paired with other evidence like textural analysis.

name: Eddie Spagnuolo
title: From aquatic ferns to rainforest trees: The first plant macrofossils from the early Eocene Ghazij Formation record adiverse flora and associated insect herbivory on the Indian Subcontinent
authors: Edward J. Spagnuolo^{1}, Peter Wilf^{1}, P. J. Przybylski^{1}, L. Alejandro Giraldo^{1}, Munir ul-Haq^{2}, Scott L. Wing^{3}, William C. Clyde^{4}
institutions:
^{1}Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania, 16802, USA.
^{2}Geological Survey of Pakistan, Islamabad, Pakistan.
^{3}Department of Paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution, Washington DC, 20560, USA.
^{4}Department of Earth Sciences, University of New Hampshire, Durham, New Hampshire, 03824, United States.
abstract: Well-dated plant fossils from tropical Asia are rare, limiting understanding of how and when this region attained its floral composition and high species richness. Here, we report the first plant macrofossils and associated insect damage from the early Eocene Ghazij Formation (Balochistan, Pakistan), well known for its mammalian faunas that document early biotic interchange associated with the India (Indo-Pakistan)-Asia collision. The macrofossils were collected from 15 sites from the middle and upper Ghazij, totaling 420 compression specimens, primarily of leaves, dating to the early Eocene Climatic Optimum (EECO). The flora has an estimated 40 species, dominated by Sapindaceae (maple, lychee family) leaflets affiliated to the rainforest tree *{Pometia}, and multiple Fabaceae (legume family) and Arecaceae (palm) morphotypes. The *{Pometia-}like leaflets are the oldest macrofossils potentially affiliated to the genus and would support its proposed Indian biogeographic history based on prior pollen data. Rarer morphotypes include Menispermaceae (moonseeds), possible Rhamnaceae (buckthorns), possible *{Calophyllum, }Araceae (*{Monstera} family), *{}and the aquatic ferns *{Acrostichum }and*{ Salvinia}.Insect-feeding damage is diverse and abundant, totaling 47 damage types (DTs), including nine hole feeding DTs, seven piercing and sucking DTs, 13 gall DTs, and six mines. Adjusted for sample size, the Ghazij flora has some of the highest herbivory levels in the fossil record (although mining is rare), providing novel information about tropical plant-animal interactions during the EECO.

name: Dani Buchheister
title: The iron-sulfur world in a bottle: FeS_{2}formation in microbial enrichment cultures
authors: Dani Buchheister^{1}, Kenneth Broad^{2}, Nadir Quarta^{3}, Julie Cosmidis^{4}, Jennifer Macalady^{1}
institutions:
^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{2}Department of Environmental Science and Policy, University of Miami, Coral Gables, FL, USA
^{3}QUARTADimensione, Switzerland
^{4}Department of Earth Sciences, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK
abstract: The Frasassi cave system in central Italy hosts a permanently stratified sulfidic aquifer with a shallow microoxic zone and a deeper anoxic zone. The deep aquifer lacks most of the oxidants used for respiration by surface life, and has sulfate concentrations of approximately one-eighth of marine, making it a promising analog for Proterozoic oceans. Biofilms in the deep aquifer contain abundant pyrite (FeS, ) mineral grains and a treasure trove of microbial “dark matter, ” microorganisms with only distant relatives in public databases. There are multiple formation pathways for FeS2, and the role that microbes play in iron sulfide mineral nucleation and crystal growth is the topic of ongoing debate.\nIn February 2023, Frasassi deep aquifer biofilms were retrieved to inoculate enrichment cultures targeting a “missing” metabolism–Wächtershäuser’s proposed pyrite- and hydrogen-producing metabolism that reacts iron sulfide (FeS) with hydrogen sulfide. After a year of incubation, clusters of cells and micro spheroidal mineral grains were observed with transmitted light and epifluorescence microscopy. Further imaging and mineral analyses were performed using Raman spectroscopy and SEM-EDS. DNA extracted from the biofilm (inoculum) and the enrichment cultures were analyzed using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing to determine the taxonomy of the major populations. Metagenomic sequences were also obtained for the enrichment culture. Raman and SEM-EDS data indicate the presence of FeS_{2} in the enrichment culture bottles but not in the abiotic controls. FeS_{2}mineral grains are micro spheroidal but do not look like microbially-mediated pyrite produced in other laboratory studies. The enrichment communities show changes in taxonomic structure from the native biofilm and are much less diverse. Known sulfur cyclers are abundant in the bottles, yielding clues to the potential role of the enrichment microbes in FeS_{2} formation.

name: Sarah Jonathan
title: Measuring weathering rates across elevational gradients in climate and slope in the Sierra Nevada and Inyo Mountains of California
authors: Sarah R. Jonathan^{1}, Roman A. DiBiase^{1}, Lee B. Corbett^{2}, Paul Bierman^{2}
institutions: ^{1}Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}University of Vermont, Rubenstein School of Natural resources and the Environment
abstract: In mountain regions, where steep topography dominates, hillslopes often have a mixed surface cover, with patches of soil interspersed with bare bedrock. While this patchy surface cover is prevalent, the processes that control the breakdown – and thereby determine the persistence and extent of soil cover – are poorly constrained. Ultimately, the balance between soil loss, consisting of both physical erosion and chemical weathering, and soil production determines the extent of soil cover. However, both weathering and erosion can vary dramatically and may be influenced by a variety of factors, including climate, hillslope morphology, and tectonic setting. Here, I examine the extent and rate of weathering across ridgeline transects in three California sites spanning a range of bedrock exposures, slopes, and elevations: The Olancha Peak and Sacatar Wilderness areas in the Eastern Sierra Nevada and McElvoy Canyon in the Inyo Mountains. All three sites are underlain by granitic bedrock and experience similar altitudinal variations in climate and vegetation, but have different patterns of bedrock exposure. In the Sacatar Wilderness bedrock exposure is low and increases with elevation, while McElvoy Canyon demonstrates an inverse pattern of decreasing bedrock with increasing elevation. The Olancha Peak area occupies a middle ground with high bedrock exposure at all elevations. Across these landscapes, I use paired soil and bedrock samples to measure the extent of chemical weathering and, combined with a slope-based erosion rate model, calculate weathering rates. These values are combined with Lidar analyses of bedrock exposure and hillslope morphology and measures of soil depth to explore how weathering rates and soil production vary with soil cover across elevations. Initial results suggest that the extent of chemical weathering initially increases, then decreases with increasing elevation and the variability in weathering increases as slope steepen to the point of significant bedrock exposure.
